content.title: About
content.content: Fruit cheesecake is a dessert made from cream cheese, eggs, and sugar, topped with fresh or canned fruit. It has a smooth, creamy texture and the fruit layer adds natural sweetness and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest cheesecake recipes date back to ancient Greece, where they used cheese called feta.
The modern New York‑style cheesecake became popular in the early 20th century.
Fruits on cheesecake are often presented as a glaze, compote, or fresh slices.
Cheesecake can be made without baking, using a cookie‑butter crust.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cream cheese is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Cheese and eggs provide complete protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and cheese contain vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from fruit
items.content: Fresh berries and fruit supply vitamin C and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Probiotic effect
items.content: Certain cream cheeses (e.g., cottage cheese) contain live cultures that support gut microbiota.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar increase calories and can affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream cheese contains lactose, which may cause discomfort for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk or whey proteins should avoid cheesecake.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Cream cheese is high in saturated fat, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cheesecake chilled, sliced into portions. Pair it with berry sauce, honey, or fresh fruit. For a lighter version, use low‑fat cottage cheese and sugar substitutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cheesecake in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C, covered with plastic wrap. Consume within 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit scones are soft, lightly sweet British biscuits that incorporate pieces of fresh or dried fruit (such as raisins, cranberries, or blueberries) into the dough. They are commonly served with tea or coffee and can be either mildly sweet or slightly tart depending on the fruit used.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scones originated in Scotland in the 19th century and quickly became popular throughout England.
Traditional scones are leavened with baking powder rather than yeast, giving them a denser texture than cupcakes.
Fruit scones are often finished with a dusting of powdered sugar or a light glaze.
In the United States the closest counterpart is the muffin, though scones are usually less sweet and more crumbly.
Scones are traditionally served with clotted cream and jam.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: The fruit adds dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides B1, B2, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Berries and dried fruits are rich in antioxidants such as vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many baked goods, scones typically contain a modest amount of butter, making them lower in saturated fat.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: The combination of whole grains and fruit yields a slower rise in blood sugar than refined white bread.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional scone recipes use wheat flour, which can be problematic for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit additions and occasional added sugar increase the calorie count and may be unsuitable for diabetics.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite modest fat levels, scones are still relatively calorie‑dense due to carbohydrates and butter.

items.title: Dried fruit additives
items.content: Some dried fruits contain added sugars or preservatives; choose unsweetened varieties when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fruit scones are best served warm, split in half and spread with butter, clotted cream, or jam. They make a convenient snack, a breakfast accompaniment, or a light dessert.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store scones in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven or toaster before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Minestrone is a hearty Italian vegetable soup made with seasonal vegetables, legumes, pasta or rice, and aromatic herbs. It is known for its rich flavor and nutritional value, as well as its flexibility—any combination of ingredients can be used.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “minestrone” comes from the Italian “minestra” meaning “soup”, with the augmentative suffix “-one” indicating a large soup.
Traditional recipes vary by Italian region and season, so each cook can add their favorite vegetables.
Classic versions often use cannellini beans, but any type of bean can be substituted.
Minestrone is commonly finished with grated Parmesan cheese and fresh parsley.
The soup is a symbol of Italian home cooking and is frequently prepared in large pots for family meals.

items.title: Rich in vegetables
items.content: Minestrone provides a wide range of vegetables that are sources of vitamins A, C, K, and folate.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Legumes and vegetables supply fiber that supports healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The soup is typically prepared with minimal added oil, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Beans and, when used, pasta or rice deliver a complete set of essential amino acids.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Tomatoes, carrots, and greens contain lycopene, beta‑carotene, and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans or peas used in the soup.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using prepared broth or adding salt can raise sodium levels; it is advisable to monitor salt usage.

items.title: Tomato acidity
items.content: Tomatoes can increase stomach acidity, which may be problematic for people with gastritis.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve minestrone hot, topped with grated Parmesan cheese and fresh herbs. A slice of toasted bread or croutons can be added for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat on the stove, adding a splash of water or broth to restore the desired consistency.
